claim: Vision is drastically reduced at the time of saccades.
source: Vision is drastically reduced at the time of saccades.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript showing elevated displacement discrimination thresholds during saccades.

claim: Displacement discrimination thresholds of observers were high after participants were exposed to an intra-saccadic disturbance.
source: Displacement discrimination thresholds of observers were high after participants were exposed to an intra-saccadic disturbance.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3, where thresholds were elevated following intra-saccadic displacement contexts.

claim: After exposure to a post-saccadic disturbance or a context without any intra-saccadic stimulation, displacement discrimination improved such that observers were able to see shifts as during fixation.
source: However, after exposure to a post-saccadic disturbance or a context without any intra-saccadic stimulation, displacement discrimination improved such that observers were able to see shifts as during fixation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3H showing that thresholds decreased to near-fixation levels after post-saccadic or no-motion contexts.

claim: Saccade-contingent habituation might explain why we do not perceive trans-saccadic retinal stimulation during saccades.
source: Saccade-contingent habituation might explain why we do not perceive trans-saccadic retinal stimulation during saccades.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings, proposing a mechanism to explain the observed phenomena.

claim: Every time we perform a saccade the external world sweeps with high speed motion across the retina.
source: Every time we perform a saccade the external world sweeps with high speed motion across the retina.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the consequences of saccadic eye movements on retinal stimulation.

claim: Learning sensorimotor contingencies requires a signal that indicates the initiation of a movement.
source: Learning sensorimotor contingencies requires a signal that indicates the initiation of a movement.
evidence: This is based on established theoretical frameworks in sensorimotor control.

claim: Neurons in the intra-parietal cortex shift their receptive fields predictively, triggered by an efference copy signal.
source: To guarantee the spatial alignment across saccades between internal and external space, neurons in the intra-parietal cortex (Duhamel et al., 1992), in the frontal eye fields (Umeno and Goldberg, 1997), the superior colliculus (Walker et al., 1995) and in visual areas V2 and V3 (Nakamura and Colby, 2002) shift their receptive fields predictively, triggered by an efference copy signal (Sommer and Wurtz, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Neurons in the frontal eye fields shift their receptive fields predictively, triggered by an efference copy signal.
source: To guarantee the spatial alignment across saccades between internal and external space, neurons in the intra-parietal cortex (Duhamel et al., 1992), in the frontal eye fields (Umeno and Goldberg, 1997), the superior colliculus (Walker et al., 1995) and in visual areas V2 and V3 (Nakamura and Colby, 2002) shift their receptive fields predictively, triggered by an efference copy signal (Sommer and Wurtz, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Umeno and Goldberg, 1997.

claim: Neurons in the superior colliculus shift their receptive fields predictively, triggered by an efference copy signal.
source: To guarantee the spatial alignment across saccades between internal and external space, neurons in the intra-parietal cortex (Duhamel et al., 1992), in the frontal eye fields (Umeno and Goldberg, 1997), the superior colliculus (Walker et al., 1995) and in visual areas V2 and V3 (Nakamura and Colby, 2002) shift their receptive fields predictively, triggered by an efference copy signal (Sommer and Wurtz, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Walker et al., 1995.

claim: Neurons in visual areas V2 and V3 shift their receptive fields predictively, triggered by an efference copy signal.
source: To guarantee the spatial alignment across saccades between internal and external space, neurons in the intra-parietal cortex (Duhamel et al., 1992), in the frontal eye fields (Umeno and Goldberg, 1997), the superior colliculus (Walker et al., 1995) and in visual areas V2 and V3 (Nakamura and Colby, 2002) shift their receptive fields predictively, triggered by an efference copy signal (Sommer and Wurtz, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nakamura and Colby, 2002.

claim: The visual system is able to detect high-speed motion.
source: As it has been shown that the visual system is able to detect high-speed motion (Burr et al., 1982), the question arises why we are not aware of the motion stimulation produced by a saccade.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Burr et al., 1982.

claim: Sensitivity of visual contrast drops down at the time of saccades.
source: In the search for a mechanism that cancels trans-saccadic motion perception, researchers have found that sensitivity of visual contrast (Volkmann et al., 1978) and of motion (Burr et al., 1982; Shioiri and Cavanagh, 1989; Ilg and Hoffmann, 1993) drops down at the time of saccades.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Volkmann et al., 1978.

claim: Sensitivity of motion drops down at the time of saccades.
source: In the search for a mechanism that cancels trans-saccadic motion perception, researchers have found that sensitivity of visual contrast (Volkmann et al., 1978) and of motion (Burr et al., 1982; Shioiri and Cavanagh, 1989; Ilg and Hoffmann, 1993) drops down at the time of saccades.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burr et al., 1982; Shioiri and Cavanagh, 1989; Ilg and Hoffmann, 1993.

claim: Saccade omission amounts to 0.5–1 log units.
source: This process - called saccade omission - amounts to 0.5–1 log units, is strongest for low spatial frequencies (Volkmann, 1986; Burr et al., 1994) and is homogeneous across the visual field (Knöll et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a quantitative claim about the magnitude of saccade omission, supported by citations.

claim: Saccade omission is strongest for low spatial frequencies.
source: This process - called saccade omission - amounts to 0.5–1 log units, is strongest for low spatial frequencies (Volkmann, 1986; Burr et al., 1994) and is homogeneous across the visual field (Knöll et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Volkmann, 1986; Burr et al., 1994.

claim: Saccade omission is homogeneous across the visual field.
source: This process - called saccade omission - amounts to 0.5–1 log units, is strongest for low spatial frequencies (Volkmann, 1986; Burr et al., 1994) and is homogeneous across the visual field (Knöll et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Knöll et al., 2011.

claim: Saccade omission starts ~50 ms before saccade initiation, peaks around saccade onset and fades away 50 ms later.
source: It starts ~50 ms before saccade initiation, peaks around saccade onset and fades away 50 ms later (Volkmann et al., 1978).
evidence: This temporal characterization is supported by citation to Volkmann et al., 1978.

claim: The intra-saccadic decrease of visual sensitivity is the signature of a mechanism that shuts down the magnocelullar pathway at an early neural level to prevent the disturbing motion experience during saccades.
source: It has been argued that the intra-saccadic decrease of visual sensitivity is the signature of a mechanism that shuts down the magnocelullar pathway at an early neural level to prevent the disturbing motion experience during saccades (Burr et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from prior literature, supported by citation to Burr et al., 1994.

claim: Motion detection during saccades is still possible if stimuli are optimized for high-speed motion detection.
source: However, in contrast to an early shut-down resulting in motion blindness, Castet and Masson (2000) have demonstrated that motion detection during saccades is still possible if stimuli are optimized for high-speed motion detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Castet and Masson, 2000.

claim: The ability to perceive intra-saccadic motion depended on the difference between the peak eye velocity and grating speed.
source: They used low-contrast gratings drifting at a constant high speed (360 dva/s) and found that the ability to perceive intra-saccadic motion depended on the difference between the peak eye velocity and grating speed.
evidence: This claim describes findings from Castet and Masson's work, supported by the preceding citation context.

claim: The magnocellular pathway is still active at the time of saccades.
source: In their view, the magnocellular pathway is still active at the time of saccades and the peri-saccadic reduction of contrast sensitivity results from retinal factors (Castet et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from prior literature, supported by citation to Castet et al., 2002.

claim: The peri-saccadic reduction of contrast sensitivity results from retinal factors.
source: In their view, the magnocellular pathway is still active at the time of saccades and the peri-saccadic reduction of contrast sensitivity results from retinal factors (Castet et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from prior literature, supported by citation to Castet et al., 2002.

claim: The ability to perceive fast intra-saccadic motion declined when additional pre- and post-saccadic stimuli were visible.
source: In a follow-up study the same authors could further show that this ability to perceive fast intra-saccadic motion declined when additional pre - and post-saccadic stimuli were visible.
evidence: This claim describes findings from a follow-up study by Castet and colleagues, inferred from the context.

claim: Static images masked intra-saccadic motion thus reducing awareness.
source: They suggested that these static images masked intra-saccadic motion thus reducing awareness.
evidence: This is an interpretation from prior research, inferred from the context of Castet's work.

claim: Masking might cancel the retinal smear produced by the saccade.
source: An earlier report already showed that masking might cancel the retinal smear produced by the saccade (Campbell and Wurtz, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Campbell and Wurtz, 1978.

claim: Smear-masking survived a dichoptic presentation thus suggesting a central origin.
source: Duyck et al. (2016) recently devised a method to test the perception of intra-saccadic smear objectively and thereby corroborated the idea that masking hides saccade-induced motion from perception. In that study smear-masking survived a dichoptic presentation thus suggesting a central origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Duyck et al., 2016.

claim: Motion perception is much less salient in the presence of static objects during simulated saccades.
source: Recently, Duyck et al. (2018) used simulated saccades and found motion perception to be much less salient in the presence of static objects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Duyck et al., 2018.

claim: Trans-saccadic displacements of a certain size go unnoticed by the observer.
source: It is long known that trans-saccadic displacements of a certain size go unnoticed by the observer (Bridgeman et al., 1975; Niemeier et al., 2003), a phenomenon termed saccadic suppression of displacement.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bridgeman et al., 1975; Niemeier et al., 2003.

claim: The saccade covers the motion transient because the presence of motion transients leads to very high displacement sensitivity.
source: The reason for the poor displacement detection is that the saccade covers the motion transient because the presence of motion transients leads to very high displacement sensitivity (Legge and Campbell, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Legge and Campbell, 1981.

claim: The extra-retinal storage mechanism is activated only under the combined condition that an efferent copy signals the occurrence of an eye movement and visual stimulation is sensed.
source: Importantly, this storage mechanism is activated only under the combined condition that an efferent copy signals the occurrence of an eye movement and visual stimulation is sensed.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model described in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Recurring input of visual stimulation will habituate neurons in the extra-retinal storage, consequently leading to a reduced sensitivity for intra-saccadic stimulation.
source: Recurring input of visual stimulation will habituate neurons in the extra-retinal storage, consequently leading to a reduced sensitivity for intra-saccadic stimulation.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model described in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: In a context with low retinal stimulation, habituation remains weak and intra-saccadic neuronal responses to visual stimulation remain comparable to fixation.
source: In a context with low retinal stimulation, habituation remains weak and intra-saccadic neuronal responses to visual stimulation remain comparable to fixation.
evidence: This is a prediction of the proposed model illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: In a context with high retinal stimulation neurons habituate and intra-saccadic neuronal responses become weak.
source: However, in a context with high retinal stimulation neurons habituate and intra-saccadic neuronal responses become weak.
evidence: This is a prediction of the proposed model illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Psychometric functions for grating displacements presented during the saccade were far shallower indicating higher thresholds or stronger suppression.
source: Psychometric functions for grating displacements presented during the saccade were far shallower indicating higher thresholds or stronger suppression.
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Suppression magnitude was strong when in the context trials the grating shifted upwards during saccade performance.
source: Thus, suppression magnitude was strong when in the context trials the grating shifted upwards during saccade performance.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: For all observers, JNDs of the psychometric functions from intra-saccadic bins were steeper than those measured after context trials in which the grating was displaced.
source: For all observers, JNDs of the psychometric functions from intra-saccadic bins were steeper than those measured after context trials in which the grating was displaced.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: For all observers, intra-saccadic discrimination performance declined after they had performed saccades with intra-saccadic stimulation in the context trials.
source: For all observers, intra-saccadic discrimination performance declined after they had performed saccades with intra-saccadic stimulation in the context trials.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Observers demonstrated poor peri-saccadic displacement discrimination in baseline sessions where no context trials were applied.
source: Observers demonstrated poor peri-saccadic displacement discrimination as is expected if suppression is not absent.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Gratings had to be shifted upwards on average ~120 deg (phase shift) such that observers were able to tell the correct direction of the shift in baseline sessions.
source: Gratings had to be shifted upwards on average ~120 deg (phase shift) such that observers were able to tell the correct direction of the shift.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the baseline sessions shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Displacement discrimination thresholds were significantly higher when the grating was shifted peri-saccadically than before saccade initiation in baseline sessions.
source: A paired one-tailed T-test confirmed that displacement discrimination thresholds were significantly higher when the grating was shifted peri-saccadically than before saccade initiation (t(3) = −9.38, p=0.0026).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the baseline data analysis.

claim: The effect size of the difference between peri-saccadic and pre-saccadic displacement discrimination in baseline sessions was 1.7 (Cohen's d) which is considered a very large effect.
source: The effect size of this difference was 1.7 (Cohen's d) which is considered a very large effect.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the baseline data analysis.

claim: Intra-saccadic displacement discrimination thresholds were virtually identical to those of the baseline sessions if in the preceding context trials the grating was displaced during saccade execution.
source: Intra-saccadic displacement discrimination thresholds were virtually identical to those of the baseline sessions if in the preceding context trials the grating was displaced during saccade execution, that is 35 ms after saccade onset.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Thresholds decreased massively after participants performed context trials in which the displacement occurred after the saccade had landed or in which there was no displacement at all.
source: However, thresholds decreased massively after participants performed context trials in which the displacement occurred after the saccade had landed or in which there was no displacement at all.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: In sessions where the grating was shifted outside the period of saccade execution, peri-saccade displacement discrimination was almost as good as during fixation.
source: In these sessions, peri-saccade displacement discrimination was almost as good as during fixation.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Intra-saccadic stimulation in the context trials induced stronger suppression than post-saccadic/no displacement stimulation.
source: A paired one-tailed T-test confirmed that intra-saccadic stimulation in the context trials induced stronger suppression than post-saccadic/no displacement stimulation (t(3) = 3.68, p=0.017).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in biases between fixation and peri-saccade discrimination in baseline sessions.
source: A paired one-tailed T-test did not reveal a significant differences (t(3) = −1.63, p=0.20).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the baseline data analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: No significant difference in biases between conditions was found in the discrimination data that followed context trials.
source: Similarly in the discrimination data that followed context trials, no significant difference in biases between conditions was found (see Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: There was no evidence for a motion after-effect in the current data that would have manifested in changed bias.
source: Thus, there was no evidence for a motion after-effect in the current data that would have manifested in changed bias, that is a shift of the psychometric functions.
evidence: This is an inference from the bias analysis results.

claim: A clear elevation of discrimination thresholds was observed only if the displacement in the context trials occurred during the saccade and had the same direction (upwards) as in the test trials.
source: A clear elevation of discrimination thresholds was observed only if the displacement in the context trials occurred during the saccade and had the same direction (upwards) as in the test trials (see Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A non-parametric repeated measures ANOVA with the factors 'displacement direction' and 'displacement time' revealed a significant main effect 'displacement direction' (F(1,4) = 15.65, p=0.017).
source: A non-parametric repeated measures ANOVA with the factors 'displacement direction' (upward/downward) and 'displacement time' (during/after saccade) revealed a significant main effect 'displacement direction' (F(1,4) = 15.65, p=0.017), confirming that thresholds were elevated selectively when the displacement direction in the context and the test trials matched.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 data analysis.

claim: The significant interaction effect (F(1,4) = 8.18, p=0.046) revealed that the selectivity was observed only when the displacement occurred during but not after saccade execution.
source: The significant interaction effect (F(1,4) = 8.18, p=0.046) revealed that the selectivity was observed only when the displacement occurred during but not after saccade execution.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 data analysis.

claim: Habituation was much stronger in the intra-saccadic period and selective for the direction of the displacement in Experiment 3.
source: As in Experiment 2, habituation was much stronger in the intra-saccadic period and selective for the direction of the displacement.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: For contexts with upward displacements, a significant main effect 'displacement time' (F(1,4) = 65.556, p<0.001) was revealed.
source: For contexts with upward displacements, a significant main effect 'displacement time' (F(1,4) = 65.556, p<0.001) and a significant interaction effect (F(1,4) = 19.883, p=0.011) was revealed, confirming that the selective decrease of discrimination occurred during but not after saccade performance.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 3 data analysis.

claim: For contexts with upward displacements, a significant interaction effect (F(1,4) = 19.883, p=0.011) was revealed.
source: For contexts with upward displacements, a significant main effect 'displacement time' (F(1,4) = 65.556, p<0.001) and a significant interaction effect (F(1,4) = 19.883, p=0.011) was revealed, confirming that the selective decrease of discrimination occurred during but not after saccade performance.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 3 data analysis.

claim: For contexts with downward displacements, a significant main effect 'displacement time' (F(1,4) = 16.337, p=0.016) was revealed.
source: For contexts with downward displacements, a significant main effect 'displacement time' (F(1,4) = 16.337, p=0.016) and a significant interaction effect (F(1,4) = 25.600, p=0.007) was revealed, confirming that the selective decrease of discrimination occurred during but not after saccade performance.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 3 data analysis.

claim: For contexts with downward displacements, a significant interaction effect (F(1,4) = 25.600, p=0.007) was revealed.
source: For contexts with downward displacements, a significant main effect 'displacement time' (F(1,4) = 16.337, p=0.016) and a significant interaction effect (F(1,4) = 25.600, p=0.007) was revealed, confirming that the selective decrease of discrimination occurred during but not after saccade performance.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 3 data analysis.

claim: Saccade suppression magnitude is strongly modulated by the recent context of intra-saccadic stimulation.
source: The results of this study clearly demonstrate that saccade suppression magnitude is strongly modulated by the recent context of intra-saccadic stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: After hundreds of saccades without intra-saccadic stimulation, observers were able to detect intra-saccadic displacements almost as good as during fixation.
source: After hundreds of saccades without intra-saccadic stimulation, observers were able to detect intra-saccadic displacements almost as good as during fixation.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: If the displacement was presented systematically within the period of saccade execution, thresholds increased drastically.
source: However, if the displacement was presented systematically within the period of saccade execution, thresholds increased drastically.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The visual system habituates context-dependent to saccade-contingent visual information.
source: The visual system habituates context-dependent to saccade-contingent visual information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Neurons might saturate to the information most prevalent in the previous saccadic context and thereby cancel out disturbing intra-saccadic stimulation.
source: Instead of a general shut-down of vision, neurons might saturate to the information most prevalent in the previous saccadic context and thereby cancel out disturbing intra-saccadic stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the findings.

claim: Any visual adaptation induced was contingent on the execution of a saccade.
source: Importantly, any visual adaptation induced was contingent on the execution of a saccade.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and results showing no habituation for post-saccadic stimulation.

claim: No habituation effect was found when the stimulation in the context trials was presented after a saccade had finished.
source: No habituation effect was found when the stimulation in the context trials was presented after a saccade had finished.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: The context dependent habituation requires an extra-retinal signal that informs visual areas about the upcoming saccade.
source: The context dependent habituation therefore requires an extra-retinal signal that informs visual areas about the upcoming saccade.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that habituation only occurs for saccade-contingent stimulation.

claim: Context-dependence would be consistent with a recent Kalman filter model of saccade suppression in which higher variance in sensory feedback yields a reduced sensory weight, thereby decreasing sensitivity.
source: Such a context-dependence would be consistent with a recent Kalman filter model of saccade suppression in which higher variance in sensory feedback yields a reduced sensory weight, thereby decreasing sensitivity (Crevecoeur and Kording, 2017).
evidence: This relates the current findings to a theoretical model from prior literature.

claim: In the Kalman filter model, the strength of saccade suppression is dynamically linked to the predicted reliability of the intra-saccadic sensory signal.
source: In the model, the strength of saccade suppression is dynamically linked to the predicted reliability of the intra-saccadic sensory signal.
evidence: This describes a feature of the Kalman filter model cited from Crevecoeur and Kording, 2017.

claim: Saturation of neuronal responses after short-term motion adaptation has been reported to occur in area MT.
source: One plausible candidate for the habituation to trans-sacadic displacements might be saturation of motion-sensitive neurons. Saturation of neuronal responses after short-term motion adaptation has been reported to occur in area MT (Priebe et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Priebe et al., 2002.

claim: Displacement detection is strong during ocular fixation but weak during saccades.
source: Displacement detection is strong during ocular fixation (Legge and Campbell, 1981) but weak during saccades (Bridgeman et al., 1975; Deubel et al., 1996; Niemeier et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: No effect of saccade adaptation trials on the displacement thresholds was observed in Collins et al. (2009).
source: In this study, no effect of saccade adaptation trials on the displacement thresholds was observed (see their Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2009.

claim: Collins et al. (2009) reported a shift of the bias in displacement detection after saccade adaptation.
source: However what they did report was a shift of the bias in displacement detection after saccade adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2009.

claim: The bias of displacement discrimination was statistically indistinguishable before and after the context trials in the current study.
source: In my study however, the bias of displacement discrimination was statistically indistinguishable before and after the context trials.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of bias data shown in Figures 3I and 3J.

claim: Saccades not only adapt to intra-saccadic jumps of the saccade target but also to displacements of the background.
source: Some studies have shown that saccades not only adapt to intra-saccadic jumps of the saccade target but also to displacements of the background (Deubel, 1991; Robinson et al., 2000; Ditterich et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deubel, 1991; Robinson et al., 2000; Ditterich et al., 2000.

claim: There was no significant change in saccade gain in any of the context sessions (context 35 ms: t(3) = 1.18, p=0.32, context 98 ms: t(3) = −0.60, p=0.59, context 187 ms: t(3) = −0.66, p=0.55, context no motion: t(3) = 0.21, p=0.85).
source: I calculated one-tailed paired t-tests separately for all four sessions. There was no statistical evidence for a significant gain change in any of the sessions (context 35 ms: t(3) = 1.18, p=0.32, context 98 ms: t(3) = −0.60, p=0.59, context 187 ms: t(3) = −0.66, p=0.55, context no motion: t(3) = 0.21, p=0.85).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the saccade gain analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: An increase of visual sensitivity starting around 50 ms before saccade onset can be observed at the focus of attention, that is the saccade target.
source: An increase of visual sensitivity starting around 50 ms before saccade onset can be observed at the focus of attention, that is the saccade target (Rolfs and Carrasco, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rolfs and Carrasco, 2012.

claim: Suppression of trans-saccadic displacements is determined by peri-saccadic suppression of contrast sensitivity.
source: It has been suggested that suppression of trans-saccadic displacements is determined by peri-saccadic suppression of contrast sensitivity.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from prior literature, mentioned without specific citation.

claim: An active mechanism transiently shuts down the magnocellular pathway and thereby prevents an intra-saccadic motion sensation.
source: In this view, an active mechanism transiently shuts down the magnocellular pathway and thereby prevents an intra-saccadic motion sensation (Burr et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from prior literature, supported by citation to Burr et al., 1994.

claim: The direction selectivity found in the current study suggests that different saccade vectors are connected to habituation of different displacement directions.
source: The direction-selectivity that I found suggests that different saccade vectors are connected to habituation of different displacement directions.
evidence: This is an inference from the direction-selectivity results shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Contrast suppression and the neural modulations in area MT are absent when tested under dark conditions.
source: It has been repeatedly reported that contrast suppression (Brooks and Fuchs, 1975; Brooks et al., 1980; Mitrani et al., 1971; Richards, 1969) and the neural modulations in area MT (Price et al., 2005) are absent when tested under dark conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Intra-saccadic motion becomes visible if the light is switched on only during execution of the saccade.
source: Consistently, intra-saccadic motion becomes visible if the light is switched on only during execution of the saccade (Campbell and Wurtz, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Campbell and Wurtz, 1978.

claim: Suppression remains strong when saccades are made under ocular diffuser or in a Ganzfeld.
source: However, suppression remains strong when saccades are made under ocular diffuser or in a Ganzfeld (Riggs and Manning, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Riggs and Manning, 1982.

claim: The visual system can habituate to intra-saccadic motion only under light conditions, thus probably explaining the absence of suppression in the dark.
source: The visual system can habituate to intra-saccadic motion only under light conditions, thus probably explaining the absence of suppression in the dark.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cited findings about dark vs. light conditions.

claim: Subjects were seated 45 cm from a Eizo FlexScan T57S with the head stabilized by a forehead rest.
source: Subjects were seated 45 cm from a Eizo FlexScan T57S with the head stabilized by a forehead rest.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the apparatus section.

claim: The visible screen diagonal was 20 in., resulting in a visual field of 40 dva × 30 dva.
source: The visible screen diagonal was 20 in., resulting in a visual field of 40 dva × 30 dva.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the apparatus section.

claim: Stimuli were presented on the monitor with a vertical frequency of 120 Hz on a homogeneous gray background.
source: Stimuli were presented on the monitor with a vertical frequency of 120 Hz on a homogeneous gray background.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the apparatus section.

claim: Four subjects participated in the context-selectivity experiment (2 female, 2 male, mean age: 28; 3 naive to the purpose of each condition and the author).
source: Four subjects participated in the context-selectivity experiment (2 female, 2 male, mean age: 28; 3 naive to the purpose of each condition and the author)
evidence: This is a methodological detail about participants in Experiment 1.

claim: Five subjects participated in Experiment 2 (3 female, 2 male, mean age: 29; 4 different subjects than in Experiment 1 and naive to the purpose of each condition and the author).
source: five subjects in Experiment 2 (3 female, 2 male, mean age: 29; 4 different subjects than in Experiment 1 and naive to the purpose of each condition and the author)
